sun.summary: The star at the centre of our solar system, a ball of hot plasma holding 99.8% of its mass.
sun.learn: The Sun turns about 600 million tonnes of hydrogen into helium every second in its core, where temperatures reach some 15 million °C. The energy takes many thousands of years to work its way out to the visible surface, then just over eight minutes to reach Earth. Sunspots, flares and coronal mass ejections follow a roughly eleven-year cycle of magnetic activity, and the charged particles they release drive the aurorae.
sun.observing: Never look at the Sun directly or through unfiltered optics, which can cause permanent eye damage in moments. Use certified solar viewers or filters fitted to the front of the instrument, and only during a total eclipse's totality is it safe to look without protection.

moon.summary: Earth's only natural satellite, and the brightest object in the night sky.
moon.learn: The Moon most likely formed from debris after a Mars-sized body struck the young Earth about 4.5 billion years ago. Tidal forces have locked its rotation to its orbit, so one hemisphere always faces us. The dark plains, called maria, are ancient basalt flows, and the bright highlands are older crust scarred by impacts. Tidal friction is slowly pushing the Moon away from Earth by about 3.8 cm a year.
moon.observing: The most dramatic detail appears along the terminator, the line between day and night, where low sunlight throws long shadows. Crater walls stand out clearly around first and last quarter, while a full Moon looks flat. Even small binoculars show craters and the maria.

mercury.summary: The smallest planet and the closest to the Sun, hurrying around it every 88 days.
mercury.learn: Mercury has almost no atmosphere, so its surface swings between about 430 °C by day and −180 °C by night. Its enormous iron core makes up most of its radius, and its heavily cratered face resembles the Moon's. Because it rotates three times for every two orbits, a single solar day there lasts two Mercurian years.
mercury.observing: Mercury never strays far from the Sun, so look low in the twilight just after sunset or before sunrise around greatest elongation. A clear, flat horizon helps. Through a telescope it shows phases like a tiny Moon.

venus.summary: The brightest planet, wrapped in clouds of sulfuric acid above a searing surface.
venus.learn: Venus is nearly Earth's twin in size, but a runaway greenhouse effect under its dense carbon dioxide atmosphere holds the surface near 465 °C, hotter than Mercury. Surface pressure is about 92 times Earth's. Venus rotates backwards, and so slowly that its day is longer than its year.
venus.observing: Often called the evening or morning star, Venus outshines everything except the Sun and Moon. A small telescope reveals its phases, which were among Galileo's early evidence that planets orbit the Sun. It looks best in twilight, before the sky is dark enough for its glare to overwhelm the view.

mars.summary: The Red Planet, a cold desert world with the largest volcano in the solar system.
mars.learn: Mars owes its color to iron oxide in its dust. Olympus Mons rises some 22 km above the surrounding plains, and the Valles Marineris canyon system would span the United States. Dry river valleys and minerals formed in water show that liquid water once flowed on its surface. Its two small moons, Phobos and Deimos, may be captured asteroids or debris from an ancient impact.
mars.observing: Mars is at its largest and brightest around opposition, roughly every 26 months. Near opposition a telescope can show polar caps and dark surface markings. At other times it appears as a small orange disc.

jupiter.summary: The largest planet, a gas giant with more mass than all the others combined.
jupiter.learn: Jupiter's banded clouds are ammonia ice carried in powerful jet streams, and the Great Red Spot is a storm larger than Earth that has raged for centuries. Its four largest moons, discovered by Galileo in 1610, are worlds in their own right: volcanic Io, ice-covered Europa with its subsurface ocean, giant Ganymede, and cratered Callisto. Jupiter completes a rotation in under ten hours, the fastest of any planet.
jupiter.observing: Steady binoculars show the four Galilean moons as points of light in a line, and their positions change from night to night. A small telescope adds the two main cloud belts. Jupiter is a rewarding target for most of the year.

saturn.summary: The ringed planet, whose bright system of ice particles spans 280,000 km but is mostly just metres thick.
saturn.learn: Saturn is so light for its size that its average density is below that of water. Its rings are made of countless pieces of water ice, from dust grains to house-sized boulders. Titan, its largest moon, is the only moon with a thick atmosphere and has lakes of liquid methane, and Enceladus sprays water from an ocean under its icy crust.
saturn.observing: Any telescope magnifying around 25× shows the rings, and it is often the view that hooks people on astronomy. The rings' tilt changes over Saturn's 29-year orbit: twice per orbit they turn edge-on and nearly vanish from view.

uranus.summary: An ice giant tipped on its side, circling the Sun at nearly 3 billion km.
uranus.learn: Uranus was the first planet discovered with a telescope, by William Herschel in 1781. Its rotation axis is tilted about 98°, so each pole spends decades in sunlight and then decades in darkness. Methane in its atmosphere absorbs red light and gives the planet its pale blue-green color. It has a faint ring system and many moons named after characters from Shakespeare and Pope.
uranus.observing: At magnitude 5.7 Uranus is just within reach of the naked eye under a dark sky, though most people need binoculars and a good chart. A telescope shows a tiny, pale blue-green disc.

neptune.summary: The most distant planet, a deep-blue ice giant with the fastest winds in the solar system.
neptune.learn: Neptune was found in 1846 where mathematics predicted it should be, from small disturbances in the orbit of Uranus. Winds there have been measured at over 2,000 km/h. Its largest moon, Triton, orbits backwards, which suggests it was captured from the Kuiper Belt. Only Voyager 2 has ever visited, flying past in 1989.
neptune.observing: Neptune is too faint for the naked eye at around magnitude 7.8. Binoculars show it as a star-like point, which you can only confirm by plotting its slow motion against the background stars. A moderate telescope reveals a tiny blue disc.

constellations.And: The chained maiden, rescued by Perseus
constellations.Car: The keel of the ship Argo
constellations.Pup: The stern of the ship Argo
constellations.Vel: The sails of the ship Argo

32349.note: The brightest star in the night sky, shining so strongly because it is one of our nearest neighbours. A faint white dwarf companion, Sirius B, orbits it every 50 years.

30438.note: The second-brightest star in the night sky, a luminous supergiant far more distant than Sirius. Spacecraft have used it as a navigation reference.

69673.note: The brightest star in the northern celestial hemisphere, an orange giant moving unusually fast against the background stars. Find it by following the arc of the Big Dipper's handle.

71683.note: The closest star system to the Sun visible to the naked eye. It is a pair of Sun-like stars orbiting each other every 80 years, with faint Proxima Centauri nearby.

91262.note: One of the sky's reference stars, long used as the zero point of the magnitude scale. It rotates so quickly that it bulges at the equator, and it will be the pole star again in about 12,000 years.

24608.note: A pair of yellow giant stars so close together that they appear as one point of light, the brightest star in Auriga.

24436.note: A blue supergiant marking Orion's foot, tens of thousands of times more luminous than the Sun.

37279.note: One of the nearest bright stars. Its name means 'before the dog', because it rises just ahead of Sirius at northern latitudes.

27989.note: A red supergiant so large it would swallow Mars's orbit if placed at the Sun. It varies in brightness and dimmed noticeably in 2019–2020, and will eventually end as a supernova.

7588.note: A hot blue star spinning so rapidly that it is markedly flattened, marking the end of the river Eridanus.

97649.note: One of the closest naked-eye stars and a fast rotator. With Vega and Deneb it forms the Summer Triangle.

60718.note: The brightest star of the Southern Cross, a close multiple system.

21421.note: The orange eye of Taurus the bull. It appears among the Hyades cluster but is a foreground star, less than half as far away.

80763.note: A red supergiant at the heart of Scorpius. Its name means 'rival of Ares', from its Mars-like color.

65474.note: A close pair of hot blue stars, so tight that they distort each other's shape. The brightest star in Virgo.

37826.note: An orange giant and the brighter of Gemini's twin stars. It has a confirmed planet of its own.

113368.note: A nearby white star surrounded by a broad ring of debris, sometimes called the loneliest bright star for how empty its surrounding sky is.

102098.note: An extremely luminous blue-white supergiant, among the most intrinsically powerful stars visible to the naked eye. It marks the tail of Cygnus the swan.

49669.note: The heart of Leo, spinning so fast that it is close to breaking apart. It lies almost exactly on the ecliptic, so the Moon and planets often pass nearby.

11767.note: The North Star, lying less than a degree from the celestial pole, so it hardly moves as the sky turns. Its altitude is close to your latitude, which has guided navigators for centuries. It is a Cepheid variable, not an especially bright star.

65378.note: The middle star in the handle of the Big Dipper, with a fainter companion, Alcor, visible to sharp eyes. A telescope splits Mizar itself into two stars.

14576.note: The Demon Star, an eclipsing binary that dims noticeably every 2.87 days as its fainter companion passes in front.

10826.note: The prototype of long-period variables. It swings from naked-eye visibility to invisible and back about every 332 days.

36850.note: An extraordinary system of six stars bound together, appearing as a single point to the naked eye.

95947.note: The head of Cygnus, and one of the sky's most beautiful double stars in a small telescope: a golden primary and a sapphire-blue companion.

68756.note: The pole star when the Egyptian pyramids were built. Earth's axis wobbles over 26,000 years, moving the pole among the stars.

87937.note: A faint red dwarf with the largest proper motion of any star, crossing a Moon's width of sky in about 180 years. Only the Alpha Centauri system is closer.

70890.note: The nearest star to the Sun, a faint red dwarf far too dim to see without a telescope. It has at least one planet in its habitable zone.

25336.note: The hot blue star at Orion's left shoulder.

26311.note: The central star of Orion's Belt, a blue supergiant.

26727.note: The easternmost star of Orion's Belt. The Flame Nebula and Horsehead Nebula lie just beside it.

25930.note: The westernmost star of Orion's Belt, lying very close to the celestial equator.

M1.name: Crab Nebula
M1.note: The expanding wreck of a star that Chinese astronomers saw explode in 1054. A pulsar spinning 30 times a second powers its glow.

M3.note: A rich globular cluster containing around half a million stars, an excellent spring target for small telescopes.

M4.note: One of the nearest globular clusters, sitting just west of Antares.

M5.note: Among the oldest and largest globular clusters known to orbit the Milky Way.

M6.name: Butterfly Cluster
M6.note: An open cluster whose bright stars outline a butterfly with open wings.

M7.name: Ptolemy Cluster
M7.note: A large, bright open cluster recorded by Ptolemy around 130 CE, easily seen by eye from dark skies near the tail of Scorpius.

M8.name: Lagoon Nebula
M8.note: A vast star-forming cloud visible to the naked eye from dark sites, split by a dark lane that gives it its name.

M11.name: Wild Duck Cluster
M11.note: A dense, rich open cluster. Its brightest stars form a V like a flock in flight.

M13.name: Hercules Cluster
M13.note: The finest globular cluster of the northern sky, with several hundred thousand stars packed into a ball about 145 light-years across.

M15.note: One of the densest globular clusters known, thought to have undergone core collapse.

M16.name: Eagle Nebula
M16.note: A young cluster and glowing nebula, home of the dust columns photographed by Hubble as the Pillars of Creation.

M17.name: Omega Nebula
M17.note: A bright star-forming region, also called the Swan Nebula, one of the brightest in the Milky Way.

M20.name: Trifid Nebula
M20.note: A rare combination of red emission nebula, blue reflection nebula and dark lanes that split it into three lobes.

M22.name: Sagittarius Cluster
M22.note: One of the brightest globular clusters, near the Teapot's lid in Sagittarius.

M24.name: Sagittarius Star Cloud
M24.note: Not a true cluster but a window through the Milky Way's dust onto a dense field of distant stars.

M27.name: Dumbbell Nebula
M27.note: The first planetary nebula Messier found, and one of the brightest. It is the shed outer layers of a dying Sun-like star.

M31.name: Andromeda Galaxy
M31.note: The nearest major galaxy and the most distant object most people can see with the naked eye. It contains around a trillion stars and is on course to merge with the Milky Way in billions of years.

M32.note: A compact dwarf elliptical companion of the Andromeda Galaxy.

M33.name: Triangulum Galaxy
M33.note: The third-largest galaxy in the Local Group, large but low in surface brightness, so it needs a truly dark sky.

M35.note: A large open cluster near the foot of Gemini, visible in binoculars.

M40.name: Winnecke 4
M40.note: A faint double star Messier logged while hunting a reported nebula. It is not a true deep-sky object.

M41.note: A bright open cluster just south of Sirius, visible to the naked eye from dark sites.

M42.name: Orion Nebula
M42.note: The nearest large stellar nursery and the brightest nebula in the sky, visible by eye as the middle 'star' of Orion's sword. Four young stars, the Trapezium, light it from within.

M43.note: A small companion to the Orion Nebula, separated from it by a dark lane of dust.

M44.name: Beehive Cluster
M44.note: A swarm of stars in Cancer, visible to the naked eye as a misty patch and glorious in binoculars. Galileo first resolved it.

M45.name: Pleiades
M45.note: The Seven Sisters, the most famous star cluster in the sky. Most people see six or seven stars by eye, and binoculars reveal dozens. Its young blue stars are passing through a dusty cloud.

M46.note: A rich open cluster with a planetary nebula, NGC 2438, appearing in the same field though it lies in the foreground.

M47.note: A bright, loose open cluster lying near M46 in Puppis.

M51.name: Whirlpool Galaxy
M51.note: A classic face-on spiral interacting with a smaller companion, and the first galaxy whose spiral structure was recognised.

M57.name: Ring Nebula
M57.note: A glowing shell of gas thrown off by a dying star, looking like a tiny smoke ring in a small telescope.

M63.name: Sunflower Galaxy
M63.note: A spiral with many short, patchy arms.

M64.name: Black Eye Galaxy
M64.note: A spiral with a striking dark band of dust in front of its bright nucleus.

M74.name: Phantom Galaxy
M74.note: A nearly perfect face-on spiral, faint and famously hard to see with small instruments.

M76.name: Little Dumbbell Nebula
M76.note: A small, faint planetary nebula in Perseus.

M77.name: Cetus A
M77.note: A barred spiral with an active nucleus, among the nearest of the Seyfert galaxies.

M78.note: The brightest diffuse reflection nebula in the sky, in Orion.

M81.name: Bode's Galaxy
M81.note: A grand spiral and one of the brightest galaxies in the northern sky, sharing a binocular field with M82.

M82.name: Cigar Galaxy
M82.note: An edge-on starburst galaxy, forming stars furiously after an encounter with M81.

M83.name: Southern Pinwheel Galaxy
M83.note: A bright, face-on barred spiral that has hosted many observed supernovae.

M87.name: Virgo A
M87.note: A giant elliptical at the heart of the Virgo Cluster. Its central black hole was the first ever imaged, in 2019.

M92.note: A fine globular cluster often overlooked next to M13.

M97.name: Owl Nebula
M97.note: A planetary nebula with two dark patches that resemble an owl's eyes.

M101.name: Pinwheel Galaxy
M101.note: A huge face-on spiral near the Big Dipper's handle, low in surface brightness.

M102.name: Spindle Galaxy
M102.note: Messier's entry is disputed. Many sources regard it as a mistaken re-observation of M101. The conventional identification, used here, is the lenticular galaxy NGC 5866.

M103.note: A small open cluster near Ruchbah in Cassiopeia.

M104.name: Sombrero Galaxy
M104.note: A nearly edge-on galaxy with a bright bulge and a dark dust lane that gives it the shape of a wide-brimmed hat.

M106.note: A spiral with an active central black hole, near the Hunting Dogs.

M110.note: A dwarf elliptical companion of the Andromeda Galaxy.

LMC.name: Large Magellanic Cloud
LMC.note: A satellite galaxy of the Milky Way, seen from the southern hemisphere as a detached piece of the Milky Way. It holds the Tarantula Nebula, the most active star-forming region in the Local Group.

SMC.name: Small Magellanic Cloud
SMC.note: A dwarf galaxy orbiting the Milky Way, visible to the naked eye from southern latitudes.

NGC 104.name: 47 Tucanae
NGC 104.note: The second-brightest globular cluster, a spectacular naked-eye object beside the Small Magellanic Cloud.

NGC 5139.name: Omega Centauri
NGC 5139.note: The largest and brightest globular cluster of the Milky Way, with some ten million stars. It may be the stripped core of a dwarf galaxy.

NGC 869.name: Double Cluster (h Persei)
NGC 869.note: One half of a magnificent pair of young open clusters, in the same low-power view as NGC 884.

NGC 884.name: Double Cluster (χ Persei)
NGC 884.note: The second half of the Double Cluster in Perseus, a splendid binocular object.

NGC 3372.name: Carina Nebula
NGC 3372.note: A giant star-forming region several times larger than the Orion Nebula, surrounding the massive unstable star Eta Carinae.

NGC 253.name: Sculptor Galaxy
NGC 253.note: A bright, dusty starburst spiral seen nearly edge-on, one of the easiest galaxies after Andromeda.

NGC 5128.name: Centaurus A
NGC 5128.note: A peculiar galaxy crossed by a dramatic dust lane, the result of a past merger, and one of the closest radio galaxies.

NGC 7293.name: Helix Nebula
NGC 7293.note: One of the closest planetary nebulae, large on the sky but dim, often nicknamed the Eye of God.

NGC 6543.name: Cat's Eye Nebula
NGC 6543.note: A bright planetary nebula with intricate shells of gas, close to the north ecliptic pole.

NGC 7000.name: North America Nebula
NGC 7000.note: A large emission nebula near Deneb, shaped like the continent, that shows best in wide-field photographs.

NGC 4755.name: Jewel Box
NGC 4755.note: A compact, colorful open cluster right beside Mimosa in the Southern Cross.

NGC 7789.name: Caroline's Rose
NGC 7789.note: A rich open cluster in Cassiopeia discovered by Caroline Herschel.

NGC 2024.name: Flame Nebula
NGC 2024.note: A bright emission nebula beside Alnitak in Orion's Belt, with a dark lane through its centre.

IC 2602.name: Southern Pleiades
IC 2602.note: A bright open cluster in Carina resembling the northern Pleiades, surrounding Theta Carinae.

IC 2391.name: Omicron Velorum Cluster
IC 2391.note: A bright, naked-eye open cluster in Vela.

NGC 2244.name: Rosette Cluster
NGC 2244.note: A young open cluster whose hot stars carve out and light the huge, round Rosette Nebula around it in Monoceros.

NGC 6888.name: Crescent Nebula
NGC 6888.note: A shell blown by the fierce wind of a Wolf-Rayet star in Cygnus.

NGC 6826.name: Blinking Planetary
NGC 6826.note: A small planetary nebula that seems to wink in and out as you look directly at it and then away.

NGC 3242.name: Ghost of Jupiter
NGC 3242.note: A bright planetary nebula in Hydra, similar in apparent size to Jupiter.

NGC 7662.name: Blue Snowball
NGC 7662.note: A bright, blue-green planetary nebula in Andromeda.

NGC 2392.name: Eskimo Nebula
NGC 2392.note: A planetary nebula in Gemini with a bright central star and a surrounding hood of gas.
